Navigating British Roads on Two Wheels

Reliable navigation is essential for motorcycle touring. Whether following a pre-planned route through the Scottish Highlands or improvising through the Welsh valleys, getting lost wastes precious riding time and can leave you on unsuitable roads. The right navigation setup keeps you on track and focused on enjoying the ride.

Dedicated GPS vs Phone Navigation

The choice between a dedicated motorcycle GPS unit and a smartphone is the most common navigation debate among touring riders:

  • Dedicated GPS (TomTom Rider, Garmin Zumo) — Built specifically for motorcycles with waterproof housings, sunlight-readable screens, and glove-friendly interfaces. Offline maps mean no reliance on mobile signal in remote areas. Higher cost but purpose-designed.
  • Smartphone apps (Google Maps, Calimoto, Scenic) — Free or cheap with regular updates and massive user communities. Better interface design and more features than dedicated units. But phone screens are harder to read in sunlight, vibration can damage camera sensors, and battery drain is significant.

Best Navigation Options 2026

TomTom Rider 550 — The most popular dedicated motorcycle GPS. Waterproof, glove-friendly 4.3-inch screen, and winding road routing that actively seeks out the most enjoyable roads. Connects to your intercom for voice navigation.

Garmin Zumo XT2 — Premium 6-inch screen with excellent sunlight visibility. Off-road routing capability, incident detection, and integration with Garmin's adventure routing community. The larger screen is superb for complex navigation.

Calimoto app — The best motorcycle-specific phone app. Automatically routes you along twisty, scenic roads and rates routes by curviness. The community shares their favourite rides, making route discovery effortless across the UK.

Scenic app — Excellent for pre-planning touring routes on a computer and syncing to your phone. Turn-by-turn navigation with offline map support and good integration with popular intercom systems.

Mobile signal in rural Scotland, Wales, and parts of northern England can be non-existent. Always download offline maps before heading into remote areas. A dedicated GPS with preloaded maps removes this concern entirely.

Mounting Solutions

Whichever navigation option you choose, the mount must be vibration-dampened, secure, and positioned within your natural line of sight without blocking instruments. Quad Lock and RAM mounts are the most popular phone mounting systems, while dedicated GPS units come with their own motorcycle-specific cradles. Position the screen where a quick glance gives you the information without moving your head significantly from the forward riding position.

Planning Routes at Home

The best touring navigation starts at home on a large screen. Tools like Basecamp, MyDrive, and web-based platforms like Kurviger let you craft detailed routes optimising for scenic roads and interesting stops. Export your routes as GPX files that load onto any device. Having pre-planned routes means you spend less time staring at a screen on the road and more time enjoying the scenery. keyTakeaways: Dedicated GPS units offer waterproof housings, sunlight-readable screens and offline maps for remote areas.
Phone apps like Calimoto and Scenic are cheaper and slicker but suffer glare, vibration risk and battery drain.
Winding-road routing on a TomTom Rider or Calimoto actively seeks out the best roads.
Always download offline maps before heading into rural Scotland or Wales where signal disappears.
Plan routes at home on a big screen and export as GPX files for less screen time on the road.

pros: Dedicated units survive rain and remain readable in bright sun.
Offline maps remove reliance on patchy rural mobile signal.
Curvy-road routing turns a boring A-to-B into an enjoyable ride.
cons: Dedicated GPS units are expensive compared with a phone app.
Phone screens glare in sunlight and vibration can damage camera sensors.
Navigation battery drain is significant on a long day using a phone.

faq.q: Should I use a dedicated GPS or my phone?
faq.a: A dedicated unit such as a TomTom Rider or Garmin Zumo is purpose-built with a waterproof, glove-friendly, sunlight-readable screen and offline maps, which matters in remote areas. A phone running Calimoto or Scenic is cheaper and has a slicker interface but suffers glare, battery drain and the risk of vibration damaging the camera. For serious touring in remote regions, a dedicated GPS is the safer bet.

faq.q: What happens to navigation where there is no mobile signal?
faq.a: Mobile signal in rural Scotland, Wales and parts of northern England can be non-existent. A dedicated GPS with preloaded offline maps keeps working regardless. If you use a phone, always download offline maps for your route before you set off, otherwise you can be left with a blank screen exactly where you most need directions.

faq.q: Can I plan routes at home and load them onto my device?
faq.a: Yes, and this is the best way to tour. Tools like Garmin BaseCamp, TomTom MyDrive and web platforms such as Kurviger let you craft detailed routes on a large screen, optimising for scenic roads and interesting stops. Export the route as a GPX file and load it onto almost any device, so you spend less time staring at a screen and more time riding.

faq.q: Which app finds the best twisty roads?
faq.a: Calimoto is the standout for this. It automatically routes you along twisty, scenic roads and rates them by curviness, and its community shares favourite rides across the UK. Scenic is better for careful pre-planning on a computer with offline map support, while TomTom Rider units have their own excellent winding-road routing built in.

faq.q: How should I mount the device?
faq.a: Whatever you choose, the mount must be vibration-dampened, secure and positioned in your natural line of sight without blocking instruments. Quad Lock and RAM mounts are the most popular phone systems, while dedicated GPS units come with their own cradles. Position the screen so a quick glance gives you the information without moving your head from the forward riding position.
